questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The electric field as force per unit charge
questions.learningObjective: define the electric field and state that it does not need a test charge
questions.stem: A charged object produces a field, and a small test charge placed in that field feels a force. What is the electric field at that spot, and does it need the test charge to be there?

options.text: The force per unit positive test charge, and it is there with or without one
The force on the test charge, which only exists while the test charge is there
options.misconception: defines the field as the force itself, which grows with the test charge used

options.text: The force per unit positive test charge, but only the test charge defines it
options.misconception: accepts the definition yet denies the field has an independent existence

options.text: The acceleration of the test charge, which only the test charge can define
options.misconception: substitutes acceleration for field, which drops the dependence on the charge

questions.explanation: Dividing the force by the size of the test charge cancels the test charge out, so the field is a property of the source alone and can be mapped with a test charge or without one. The force itself is not the field, because it changes if a bigger test charge is used, and the acceleration is not the field either, because it depends on how massive the test charge is. That cancellation is precisely why the field is defined the way it is.
questions.hint: Divide out the test charge and see what is left of it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: What field line density represents
questions.learningObjective: interpret field line density as a measure of field strength
questions.stem: Two sketches of the same region near a positive charge are drawn. In one the field lines are close together, and in the other they are widely spaced. What does the closeness of the lines indicate about the field?

options.text: A stronger field there, because the density of the lines represents the strength
A weaker field there, because closely spaced lines mean a slow change
options.misconception: reads crowding as weakness, the opposite of what the density means

options.text: A stronger field there, because closely spaced lines mean more charge inside
options.misconception: attributes the crowding to the amount of charge rather than the field it makes

options.text: A weaker field there, because the lines spread out as the charge escapes away
options.misconception: believes charge drains away through the field lines as they spread

questions.explanation: Field lines are drawn so that the number crossing a unit area measures the field there, which is why a sketch of a field around a point charge is densest right at the charge and thins out with distance. The crowding is a statement about the field, not about how much charge sits inside, though the two are linked because the field comes from the charge. Lines never begin or end in empty space, so charge is not escaping along them.
questions.hint: Ask what the number of lines per unit area was chosen to represent.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why an infinite sheet's field does not fall with distance
questions.learningObjective: explain why an infinite sheet's field is independent of distance
questions.stem: A point charge's field falls away as the inverse square of distance, yet an infinite uniformly charged sheet makes a field that does not change with distance at all. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: A flat sheet spreads its fixed charge over a growing area as you move away
An infinite sheet somehow carries more total charge than a point charge
options.misconception: reasons about total charge, which is infinite for the sheet and irrelevant to its field

options.text: The two cases obey different laws, so they can never be compared
options.misconception: declines the comparison instead of noticing the spreading that causes it

options.text: The sheet's field does change with distance, but far too little to measure
options.misconception: denies the result rather than explaining the constant field it produces

questions.explanation: For a point charge, doubling the distance quarters the field because the same charge is spread over four times the area of a sphere. For an infinite sheet, doubling the distance from it doubles the area of the surrounding sphere or cylinder, but it also brings twice as much of the sheet inside that surface, so the two effects cancel and the field stays constant. That is why E depends only on the surface charge density and not on where you stand.
questions.hint: Compare how much charge a surface at that distance encloses in each case.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Superposition of two equal charges
questions.learningObjective: apply superposition to find a net field between two equal charges
questions.stem: Two equal positive charges are held a short distance apart. A small positive test charge is placed exactly halfway between them, on the line joining them. What is the net electric field there?

options.text: Zero, because the two equal and opposite fields at that point cancel
Twice a single field, because both fields point away along the same line
options.misconception: adds two fields that point in opposite directions along the axis

options.text: Zero, because the test charge is screened from both source charges
options.misconception: gives the right value by crediting a shielding effect that is not present

options.text: Nonzero, because equal charges still produce fields that add up here
options.misconception: insists the magnitudes add while overlooking that the directions oppose

questions.explanation: Each positive charge pushes the test charge away from itself, so on the axis between them the nearer charge pushes one way and the farther charge pushes the other. The distances are equal so the magnitudes are equal, and equal magnitudes in opposite directions leave nothing behind. This is the simplest demonstration of superposition: fields add as vectors, and cancelling is as real a sum as reinforcing.
questions.hint: Sketch both field arrows at the midpoint before adding anything up.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Field on the axis of an electric dipole
questions.learningObjective: state the direction of a dipole's field on its axis
questions.stem: A dipole is a positive and a negative charge held a short distance apart. What is the direction of the electric field on the axis of the dipole, at a point beyond the positive charge?

options.text: Along the axis, away from the positive charge and towards the negative one
Across the axis, at right angles to the line joining the two charges
options.misconception: gives the equatorial direction where the two contributions are equal and opposite

options.text: Along the axis, from the negative charge towards the positive one
options.misconception: reverses the sense of the axial field, which is where the fields reinforce

options.text: Zero, because the two fields cancel everywhere along the axis
options.misconception: applies the equatorial cancellation to the axis, where the fields add instead

questions.explanation: On the axis beyond the positive charge, the nearer positive charge pushes strongly in one direction and the more distant negative charge pulls weakly in the same direction, so the two reinforce and the field points away from the positive end. Across the equator, by contrast, the two contributions are equal and opposite and cancel exactly along the line joining the charges. The dipole field therefore falls faster than a point charge field, as the inverse cube, because of that extra factor of distance.
questions.hint: Compare the distances from the two charges, and the direction each one pushes.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium
questions.learningObjective: explain why the field inside a conductor in equilibrium is zero
questions.stem: Free charges can move freely through a metal. A conductor carrying an excess charge is then left alone until nothing inside it is moving. What must be true of the electric field inside that conductor?

options.text: Zero everywhere inside, because any nonzero field would keep moving the free charges
Zero everywhere inside, because the excess charge sits a long way from the middle
options.misconception: gives the right field for the wrong reason, locating the charge rather than the cause

options.text: Equal to the field just outside the surface, since the field passes through metal
options.misconception: believes the field carries straight through the metal unchanged

options.text: Nonzero inside, because the excess charge repels itself through the whole body
options.misconception: believes the self-repulsion of the charge leaves a field in the bulk

questions.explanation: If the field anywhere inside the metal were nonzero, the free charges there would accelerate, which is a change of state, and the conductor would not be in equilibrium. So equilibrium requires a zero internal field, and the excess charge is pushed out to the surface until that is true. The field just outside the surface is strong and perpendicular to it, and the metal is precisely what makes the field inside zero while the field outside is not.
questions.hint: Equilibrium means nothing is moving, so ask what a nonzero field would do to free charges.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Where excess charge sits on a conductor
questions.learningObjective: state that a cavity inside a conductor carries no charge on its walls
questions.stem: A charge is placed inside the cavity of a hollow metal sphere that carries no charge of its own. Where does the charge induced on the sphere end up?

options.text: Entirely on the outer surface, with the cavity walls left neutral
Entirely on the cavity walls, keeping the outside shielded from the charge
options.misconception: puts the induced charge where the equilibrium argument forbids it

options.text: Split evenly between the inner and outer surfaces of the metal
options.misconception: splits the charge between two surfaces when only one can carry it

options.text: Spread through the metal itself, because a metal is a good conductor
options.misconception: believes good conduction helps charge move through the bulk rather than onto the surface

questions.explanation: Induced charge on the inner wall would make a field inside the metal, and free charges would immediately move to cancel it, so the inner surface ends up neutral. The induced charge appears only on the outer surface, where it raises the outside field without putting any field in the metal. The same argument explains why a charge inside a closed metal shell is invisible from outside when the shell is uncharged, and why grounding the shell lets that charge escape instead.
questions.hint: Ask whether induced charge on the inner wall is compatible with a zero field in the metal.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Grounding and induced charge
questions.learningObjective: describe the charge redistribution when a charged rod nears a grounded conductor
questions.stem: A positively charged rod is brought near an uncharged metal sphere that is touching the ground through a wire, and the rod is held there. What happens to the sphere's charges?

options.text: Electrons flow in from the ground, leaving the far side of the sphere positive
Electrons flow out to the ground, leaving the far side of the sphere positive
options.misconception: sends electrons the wrong way, so the far side ends up negative not positive

options.text: No charge moves, because the sphere is neutral and nothing has touched it
options.misconception: believes neutrality prevents any redistribution under an external field

options.text: Electrons flow in from the ground, leaving the near side of the sphere negative
options.misconception: correctly describes the arriving electrons but puts the deficit on the near side

questions.explanation: The rod's field pushes free electrons in the sphere away from the rod, towards the far side and out through the grounding wire, so the sphere is left with a deficit on the near side and an excess on the far side. The ground is the reservoir that makes this possible: without it the sphere would merely polarise, with no net charge arriving or leaving. Equilibrium is reached when the rod's field and the sphere's own induced field cancel at every free charge, which is the whole content of the rule.
questions.hint: Ask which way the rod's field pushes the sphere's own electrons, and where they can go.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Direction of the field of a current element
questions.learningObjective: apply the right-hand rule to a straight current element
questions.stem: A current element in a straight wire points along the direction of the current. Using the right-hand rule, which description gives the direction of the magnetic field it produces nearby?

options.text: Point the right thumb along the current and curl the fingers round the wire
Point the right thumb along the current and read the field from the palm
options.misconception: uses the thumb correctly but reads the direction off the palm instead of the fingers

options.text: Curl the right fingers along the current and read the direction from the thumb
options.misconception: reverses the roles of the thumb and the fingers in the rule

options.text: Point the right fingers along the current and read the field from the palm
options.misconception: aligns the fingers with the current, which is not how the rule is set up

questions.explanation: The right-hand rule for a straight current is a wrapping motion: the thumb goes along the current and the fingers curl the way the field runs, so a thumb pointing up gives a field that circles anticlockwise seen from above. Reading the direction off the palm reverses the curl and so gives the field on the wrong side of the wire, which is the classic error in applying this rule. Swapping the thumb and fingers gives the direction for a coil rather than a straight wire.
questions.hint: One finger or thumb gives the current, the curled ones give the circling field.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Field of a long straight wire
questions.learningObjective: state how the field of a long straight wire depends on distance
questions.stem: The magnetic field of a long straight wire is measured at two distances from it, with the current and everything else unchanged. What happens to the field when the distance from the wire is doubled?

options.text: It halves, because the field falls in inverse proportion to distance
It quarters, because the field falls in inverse proportion to distance
options.misconception: gives the inverse square falloff, which belongs to a point charge's electric field

options.text: It stays the same, because a wire long enough fills all the space around it
options.misconception: believes the field is uniform in the way an infinite sheet's electric field is

options.text: It doubles, because the current spreads out as the distance grows
options.misconception: assumes the field grows with distance, the opposite of any field law

questions.explanation: The field of a straight wire is B = mu_0 I over 2 pi r, so it is proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the distance, and doubling the distance halves the field. The tempting inverse square comes from the electric field of a point charge, which is a different geometry altogether. Unlike the electric field of an infinite sheet, the wire's field does vary with distance, because going further away does not bring any more current into the enclosing surface.
questions.hint: Write the field as a constant over the distance and see what happens to the fraction.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Field at the centre of a multi-turn coil
questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of increasing the number of turns of a coil
questions.stem: A circular coil carries a steady current, and the coil is then rewound with the same wire, the same current, and the same radius but twenty turns instead of one. What happens to the field at the centre?

options.text: It becomes twenty times larger, because the turns add their fields together
It stays the same, because the current and the radius have not changed
options.misconception: ignores the extra turns, which are exactly what has been changed

options.text: It becomes twenty times smaller, because each turn carries a smaller share
options.misconception: believes the same current splits between the turns, as current would in parallel

options.text: It becomes twenty times larger, because the wire resistance has fallen
options.misconception: gives the right factor but credits a change in resistance rather than the added turns

questions.explanation: At the centre every turn of the coil produces a field in the same direction, so the contributions add and the field is proportional to the number of turns, giving twenty times the single-turn value. The current does not split between the turns: they are in series round one loop, which is exactly why each carries the full current. A lower resistance may well accompany the rewinding, but the field follows from the turns, not from the resistance.
questions.hint: Ask which way each turn's field points at the centre of the coil.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The field of a solenoid
questions.learningObjective: describe where a solenoid's field lies and how it varies
questions.stem: A long solenoid carries a steady current. Where does its magnetic field actually lie, and how does that field change from the axis outwards?

options.text: Inside the windings, nearly uniform, falling to nearly zero well outside the ends
Inside the windings, nearly uniform, rising again well beyond the two ends
options.misconception: keeps the interior right but reinvents a field at infinity

options.text: Only outside the windings, where the field lines close around the axis
options.misconception: puts the field outside a solenoid rather than inside it

options.text: Only at the two ends, where the windings sit closest to the axis
options.misconception: confines the field to the ends, which is the opposite of a long solenoid's behaviour

questions.explanation: A long solenoid behaves almost exactly like a magnet, with a nearly uniform field along its axis inside the windings and a field that falls to nearly zero a short distance outside. The cancellation outside happens because the fields of the turns beyond a point all point the other way, which is the same reason an infinite sheet's field outside is zero. That near-zero external field is what makes a solenoid far better at confining a field than a single loop or a bare wire.
questions.hint: Add up the fields of many turns stacked along the axis and see where they agree.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: A motor and a generator are one machine
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a motor from a generator by the direction of energy flow
questions.stem: An electric motor and a generator can be built as the same machine, turned the other way round. What actually distinguishes the two when they are running?

options.text: A motor takes electrical power and produces mechanical force, a generator the reverse
A motor takes mechanical force and produces electrical power, a generator the reverse
options.misconception: has the two machines the wrong way round, swapping their roles

options.text: A motor needs a steady current, a generator needs a steady magnetic field
options.misconception: says each needs the part that is in fact common to both

options.text: A motor has a moving coil, a generator has a moving magnet instead
options.misconception: insists on different moving parts, when either may move in either machine

questions.explanation: The same coil in the same field does both jobs, and the force on the current-carrying conductors is exactly the reaction that would drive a current if the coil were turned instead. What differs is only which quantity is supplied and which is produced, so one machine can even be run as both, which is what regenerative braking does. Requiring a moving coil in one and a moving magnet in the other is a practical preference, not a principle.
questions.hint: Ask which way the energy flows, and ignore which part happens to be moving.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Angle dependence of the magnetic force on a charge
questions.learningObjective: state how the magnetic force on a moving charge depends on the angle
questions.stem: A charged particle moves through a uniform magnetic field, and the angle between its velocity and the field is varied while the speed and the field strength stay fixed. How does the magnetic force respond?

options.text: It is greatest at right angles and falls to zero when the motion is along the field
It is greatest along the field and falls to zero when the motion is across it
options.misconception: reverses the dependence, putting the maximum where the force actually vanishes

options.text: It is the same at every angle, because the speed and the field are unchanged
options.misconception: ignores the angle altogether, which is the one factor that was changed

options.text: It is greatest at right angles and rises again when the motion is along the field
options.misconception: keeps the correct maximum but invents a second rise at the parallel case

questions.explanation: The magnetic force is q times v times B times the sine of the angle between the velocity and the field, so it is largest at ninety degrees and vanishes when the motion is along the field lines, where the velocity and the field are parallel and the cross product is zero. A particle travelling along a field line therefore experiences no magnetic force at all, whatever its speed. That zero is a genuine physical result, not a limiting approximation.
questions.hint: Think of the force as a cross product and find where the angle makes it vanish.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Polarisation of reflected light
questions.learningObjective: state the direction of the electric field of reflected light
questions.stem: Unpolarised light strikes a smooth water surface and part of it reflects. In which direction does the electric field of the reflected beam point?

options.text: In the plane of the surface, perpendicular to the plane of incidence
In the plane of incidence, along the direction of the reflected ray
options.misconception: picks the plane that a reflected electric field cannot have, since it would drive charges out of the surface

options.text: At 45 degrees to the surface, whichever direction the light came from
options.misconception: invents a fixed tilt unrelated to the angle of incidence

options.text: In every direction at once, because the incident light is unpolarised
options.misconception: expects the reflected beam to stay unpolarised, ignoring what reflection selects

questions.explanation: Light is carried by charges oscillating in the medium, and at a conducting surface only the component of that oscillation lying in the surface can exist, so the reflected electric field must lie in the surface, perpendicular to the plane of incidence. The component along that plane cannot be matched, so it is not reflected, and the reflected beam is plane-polarised however random the incident light was. This is why a grazing reflection off water or glass is strongly polarised and why polarizing sunglasses cut that glare.
questions.hint: Ask which way the surface charges can actually oscillate when light reaches them.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Matching spectrum bands to their uses
questions.learningObjective: match each band of the spectrum to a use that depends on its frequency
questions.stem: Six bands of the electromagnetic spectrum are listed, each with one claimed use. Which pairing of a band with its use is correct?

options.text: Infrared with night-vision lamps that detect warm bodies without visible light
Radio waves with the ultraviolet lamps that sterilise instruments in an operating theatre
options.misconception: swaps the radio and ultraviolet bands, both of which are real but not in that order

options.text: X-rays with the microwave ovens that heat food from the inside outwards
options.misconception: swaps the X-ray and microwave bands, both of which are real but not in that order

options.text: Ultraviolet with the satellite links that carry telephone calls overhead
options.misconception: swaps the ultraviolet and radio bands, both of which are real but not in that order

questions.explanation: Infrared sits just below visible red, its photons are small enough to be absorbed by warm objects without being seen, and that is exactly what a night-vision lamp exploits. Choosing a band means choosing a frequency, and the use follows from what the frequency does to matter.
questions.hint: Start from the frequency of each use and work back to the band.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Field of a point charge
questions.learningObjective: compute the field of a point charge at a stated distance
questions.stem: A point charge of 2.0 microcoulombs sits in empty space. What is the electric field strength 0.30 m from it? Use k = 8.99 x 10^9 in SI units and report the answer in newtons per coulomb. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The field is k times the charge over the square of the distance, 8.99e9 times 2.0e-6 over 0.09, which is 2.0e5 newtons per coulomb. The distance has to be squared, and using 0.30 instead of 0.09 would give three times too much. The units are right by construction, since newtons per coulomb is a force per unit charge, which is the definition of the field.
questions.hint: Square the distance before dividing, and keep both quantities in SI units.

questions.topic: Field of the same charge at a greater distance
questions.learningObjective: compute the field of a point charge at a second, larger distance
questions.stem: The same point charge of 2.0 microcoulombs is measured again, this time 0.60 m from the charge. What is the field strength there, in newtons per coulomb? Use k = 8.99 x 10^9 in SI units. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Doubling the distance from 0.30 m to 0.60 m squares the denominator and so quarters the field, and 2.0e5 over 4 is 5.0e4 newtons per coulomb. Computing it directly, 8.99e9 times 2.0e-6 over 0.36, gives the same 4.99e4, which is the second route. This quartering on doubling is the signature of an inverse square law and is the quickest way to check any such answer.
questions.hint: Doubling the distance multiplies the field by the inverse of four.

questions.topic: Field of an infinite charged sheet
questions.learningObjective: compute the field of an infinite uniformly charged sheet
questions.stem: A very large flat sheet carries a uniform surface charge density of 5.0e-6 coulombs per square metre. What is the electric field just on one side of an effectively infinite sheet? Use eps_0 = 8.85e-12 F/m and report the answer in newtons per coulomb. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The field of an infinite sheet is the surface charge density over twice the permittivity, 5.0e-6 over 1.77e-11, which is 2.8e5 newtons per coulomb. The factor of two is the part most often missed, and it comes from the two sides of a Gaussian pillbox each contributing half the flux. Note also that the permittivity appears once here, not squared as it would in a capacitance formula, and that no distance enters at all.
questions.hint: Use the sheet formula, which divides the surface charge density by twice the permittivity.

The 1.0 mm separation is not needed, since the field between ideal large plates does not depend on it.

questions.topic: Capacitance of a parallel-plate pair
questions.learningObjective: compute the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor from its geometry
questions.stem: Two parallel conducting plates of area 0.20 square metres are separated by 2.0 mm of air. What is the capacitance of the pair? Use eps_0 = 8.85e-12 F/m and report the answer in picofarads. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The capacitance is the permittivity times the plate area over the gap, 8.85e-12 times 0.20 over 2.0e-3, which is 8.85e-10 F, and that is 885 picofarads. The gap has to be converted from millimetres to metres, and 2.0 mm is 2.0e-3 m. Larger plates and a smaller gap both raise the capacitance, which is why the plates are large and the separation tiny in a real capacitor.

questions.topic: Reading an inverse first power law from data
questions.learningObjective: identify an inverse first power relationship from logged field strengths
questions.stem: The field of a long straight wire is logged at four distances: 5.00e-5 T at 0.020 m, 2.50e-5 at 0.040 m, 1.67e-5 at 0.060 m, and 1.25e-5 at 0.080 m. Which relationship do those four readings follow?

options.text: Inverse first power, since every doubling of the distance halves the value
Inverse square, since every doubling of the distance cuts the value by four
options.misconception: borrows the point charge falloff, which the first doubling already rules out

options.text: Linear, since the value falls in proportion to the distance itself
options.misconception: expects equal steps in distance to give equal steps in field, which they do not

options.text: Inverse cube, since every doubling of the distance cuts the value by eight
options.misconception: borrows the dipole falloff, which needs two charges rather than one

questions.explanation: The first two readings differ by exactly a factor of two in the field for a factor of two in the distance, and the last reading is a quarter of the first for four times the distance, which is the signature of an inverse first power law. The middle entry is the one that needs a little care: at three times the distance the prediction is 5.00e-5 over 3, which is 1.67e-5, exactly as logged. An inverse square law would have predicted 5.6e-6 at that distance, well below the measured value.
questions.hint: Check the reading at three times the distance against one third and one ninth of the first.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Field line spacing against a measured force
questions.learningObjective: relate field line density to a measured force on a test charge
questions.stem: A tiny test charge of 1.0e-6 C feels a force of 4.0e-7 N at one point in a field and 1.0e-7 N at a second point two centimetres away. How should the field lines be drawn in that region?

options.text: Roughly four times closer together near the first point
Roughly four times further apart near the first point
options.misconception: reads a stronger field as a sparser drawing, the opposite of the convention

options.text: With the same spacing at both points, since the force fell for other reasons
options.misconception: assumes the field is constant and blames the change on something else

options.text: Roughly two times closer together near the first point
options.misconception: takes the ratio of the forces rather than the ratio of the fields

questions.explanation: Divide each force by the same test charge and the field strengths are 4.0e-1 and 1.0e-1 newtons per coulomb, so the field is four times stronger at the first point. Field lines are drawn with a density proportional to the field, so four times the strength means four times the lines per unit area there. Taking the ratio of the forces works here only because the test charge is the same in both places, and it is the field ratio that the drawing must show.
questions.hint: Convert both forces to field strengths before comparing them.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Charge crowding on a conductor of varying curvature
questions.learningObjective: interpret a surface charge density map of an irregular conductor
questions.stem: A conductor is made of a large sphere with a small sphere joined to it, and the whole assembly is given a net charge. A probe measures 1.0e-6 C/m^2 on the large sphere and 4.0e-6 C/m^2 on the small one. What do those two readings show?

options.text: Charge crowds where the surface curves most sharply
Charge spreads evenly, so the reading on the small sphere is an error
options.misconception: assumes a uniform spread and dismisses a factor of four as an error

options.text: Charge collects on the large sphere because it has the greater volume
options.misconception: confuses volume, which carries no charge, with surface, which carries it all

options.text: Charge stays where the two spheres touch, along the joining region
options.misconception: locates the charge on a seam rather than on the high-curvature surface

questions.explanation: The field just outside a conductor is proportional to the local surface charge density, and a small sphere has a much sharper curvature than a large one, so its surface field is stronger and more charge per unit area sits there. Four times the density on the small sphere is the expected crowding and not a fault in the probe. The total charge still belongs entirely to the surface, since a conductor in equilibrium has no field and no charge in its bulk.
questions.hint: Compare the curvature of the two surfaces, since that sets the surface field.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Intensity against electric field amplitude
questions.learningObjective: identify how intensity depends on the amplitude of a plane wave
questions.stem: A transmitter's electric field amplitude is raised from 1.0 V/m to 2.0 V/m and then to 3.0 V/m, and the measured average intensity in the far field reads 1.33e-3 W/m^2, then 5.31e-3, then 1.19e-2. What does that sequence show?

options.text: Intensity grows with the square of the field amplitude, not with the amplitude itself
Intensity grows with the field amplitude itself, in direct proportion
options.misconception: predicts a factor of two per doubling, which the second reading is not

options.text: Intensity grows with the square of the field amplitude, and doubles at each step
options.misconception: claims a constant ratio per step, which only holds for equal steps in amplitude

options.text: Intensity grows with the square root of the amplitude, so the steps shrink
options.misconception: predicts shrinking steps, whereas the measured steps grow by four and by nine

questions.explanation: Dividing through by the first reading gives factors of one, four and nine for amplitude steps of one, two and three, which is the square of the amplitude step and nothing else. The sequence agrees with the plane wave result that the average intensity is half the permittivity times the speed of light times the square of the field amplitude, and a second route with those constants gives 1.33e-3, 5.31e-3 and 1.19e-2 W/m^2 exactly as logged. A claim of direct proportion would need the second reading to be 2.66e-3.
questions.hint: Divide each intensity by the first and compare with the square of each amplitude step.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Path radius against field strength
questions.learningObjective: identify how the circular path radius depends on field strength
questions.stem: The same electron of mass 9.11e-31 kg is set moving at 2.0e6 m/s at right angles to four different uniform magnetic fields, and the path radii come out as 5.69e-5 m, 2.85e-5 m, 2.28e-5 m and 1.14e-5 m. What do the four radii show?

options.text: The radius is inversely proportional to the field strength
The radius is directly proportional to the field strength
options.misconception: predicts the radius growing with the field, which is the opposite of the trend

options.text: The radius is inversely proportional to the square of the field
options.misconception: predicts a factor of four per doubling where the data show a factor of two

options.text: The radius does not depend on the field strength at all
options.misconception: ignores the steady trend across four very different field strengths

questions.explanation: The radii halve each time the field is doubled, 5.69e-5 at 0.20 T and 2.85e-5 at 0.40 T, which is an inverse first power law, and the third reading at 0.50 T fits 2.28e-5 as well. Setting the magnetic force equal to the centripetal force gives a radius of m v over q B, in which the field appears to the first power in the denominator and the speed cancels out of the period. An inverse square law would fall much faster than the data do.
questions.hint: Halve the field and see by what factor the measured radius changes.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Capacitance and the geometry of the plates
questions.learningObjective: state the parallel-plate capacitance formula and its geometric scaling
questions.stem: Write the expression for the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor in terms of the plate area and the gap, and say what happens when the area is doubled and the gap is halved at the same time.

options.text: It is eps_0 A over d, so the capacitance rises to four times its value
It is eps_0 A over d, so the capacitance rises to two times its value
options.misconception: counts only one of the two changes instead of both of them

options.text: It is eps_0 d over A, so the capacitance falls to a quarter of its value
options.misconception: inverts the formula, which is the relation for the area needed for a given C

options.text: It is eps_0 A over d, so the capacitance is unchanged by that change
options.misconception: treats the product of area and gap as fixed rather than their ratio

questions.explanation: The capacitance is the permittivity times the plate area over the gap, so doubling the area multiplies it by two and halving the gap multiplies it by another two, giving four times the original capacitance. The two changes work in the same direction because the area and the gap enter as a ratio, and a ratio of two doublings in the numerator is a factor of four. Inverting the formula is not a different physics but a rearrangement, useful for finding the plate area a target capacitance needs.
questions.hint: Both changes are in the numerator of a ratio, so their factors multiply.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The field of an infinite charged sheet
questions.learningObjective: state the field of an infinite sheet and its distance dependence
questions.stem: Write the expression for the electric field of an infinite sheet carrying a uniform surface charge density, and say what that field does as the distance from the sheet grows.

options.text: It is sigma over twice eps_0, and it does not change with distance
It is sigma over eps_0, and it falls away as the inverse of distance
options.misconception: omits the factor of two and adds a distance dependence the geometry does not have

options.text: It is sigma over twice eps_0, and it falls away as the inverse square
options.misconception: keeps the coefficient right but gives it the falloff of a point charge

options.text: It is two sigma over eps_0, and it falls away as the inverse square
options.misconception: gets both the factor and the falloff wrong in the same answer

questions.explanation: An infinite sheet produces a field of sigma over 2 eps_0 on each side, and the field does not vary with distance, which is the striking part of the result. A Gaussian pillbox drawn around the sheet gives the same field from each side, and the closer you move the more of the sheet is enclosed, so the enclosed charge grows in step with the area. That cancellation is why an infinite sheet is used as the ideal model for one plate of a parallel-plate capacitor.
questions.hint: A Gaussian surface around the sheet is pulled out by the two faces, and the enclosed charge grows with the area.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The field of a long straight wire
questions.learningObjective: state the field of a long straight wire and the constants it contains
questions.stem: Write the expression for the magnetic field that a long straight wire carrying a current I produces at a distance r from itself, and name the constants that appear in it.

options.text: It is mu_0 I over 2 pi r, using the permeability of free space and pi
It is mu_0 I over r, using the permeability of free space and pi
options.misconception: drops the factor of two pi, which comes from the circular path length

options.text: It is eps_0 I over 2 pi r, using the permittivity of free space and pi
options.misconception: substitutes the electric constant, which cannot produce a magnetic field

options.text: It is mu_0 I over 2 pi r squared, using the permeability of free space and pi
options.misconception: gives the field the inverse square dependence of a point charge's electric field

questions.explanation: The field is the permeability of free space times the current over 2 pi r, and the two constants are the vacuum permeability and pi. The 2 pi r in the denominator is the length of the circular path a magnetic field line takes around the wire, and the field is uniform along it, so the line integral is just B times 2 pi r. A magnetic field falls as the inverse first power of distance, not the inverse square, since the geometry is a line rather than a point.
questions.hint: The denominator comes from the circumference of a circle around the wire.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The two factors in Faraday's law
questions.learningObjective: state Faraday's law and identify what sets the size of the induced emf
questions.stem: Write the expression for the emf induced in a coil of N turns when the magnetic flux through each turn changes with time, and name the two factors that set its size.

options.text: It is minus N times the rate of change of flux, set by N and the flux change rate
It is minus N times the rate of change of flux, set by N and the flux itself
options.misconception: quotes the flux rather than how fast it changes, so a steady flux would give an emf

options.text: It is minus N times the flux, set by N and the time it takes to change
options.misconception: drops the time derivative, so the emf would scale with the flux alone

options.text: It is minus the rate of change of flux, set by the flux and the time
options.misconception: omits the turn count, which multiplies the emf of every turn in the coil

questions.explanation: The induced emf is minus N times the rate of change of flux through the coil, so the two factors are the number of turns and how quickly the flux is changing, and the flux value on its own is irrelevant. Rewinding a coil with twice the turns doubles the emf at the same rate of flux change, which is exactly what a generator does when it is rewound. A steady flux, however large, induces nothing, which is the whole reason a transformer needs an alternating supply.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be changing for an emf to appear at all, and what multiplies the effect of each turn.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Lenz's law as a statement about energy
questions.learningObjective: explain induced current drag as a consequence of energy conservation
questions.stem: A conducting rod is pushed along horizontal rails at a steady speed while a strong magnet sits between them. Your hand keeps pushing at a constant force and feels a steady drag. Explain in your own words why that drag is there and where the power your hand supplies ends up.

answer.exemplar: As the rod moves, the charges in it are pushed sideways through the magnetic field, so a potential difference appears along its length and a current runs round the closed loop made by the rod and the rails. That current has its own magnetic field, and the two fields are arranged so that the new field opposes the change that produced it, which here means the force on the rod opposes the motion. Since you are holding a steady speed, your hand must supply work at exactly the rate the circuit turns that mechanical energy into heat in the rod and the rails. If the induced current had reinforced the change instead, the rod would have accelerated on its own and the circuit would have produced energy from nothing, which is the whole reason the law has the sign it does.

questions.explanation: The induced current is not a rule about sign; it is what energy conservation requires. A reinforcing current would let the circuit amplify its own motion indefinitely, so the only self-consistent possibility is the opposing one. Steady speed is the useful condition here, because it means all of your work goes into the circuit and none into speeding the rod up.
questions.hint: Ask what force opposes the motion, and which way its current must flow.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why an aerial has to be long enough to radiate
questions.learningObjective: explain the length requirement of a radiating aerial in terms of changing fields
questions.stem: A pocket radio set works well only when its aerial is roughly a quarter of the wavelength of the station it is tuned to, while a stubby aerial a few millimetres long does almost nothing. Explain in your own words what the length of the aerial has to do with radiating, using what a changing current does to the fields around it.

answer.exemplar: A current that is steady just produces a steady magnetic field around the wire, and steady fields do not radiate; what radiates is a current that changes, because accelerating charges push the electric field ahead of them and the changing electric field drags a magnetic field along with it, and the two together carry energy away. For the fields built up at one end of the aerial to reinforce those from the far end rather than cancel them, the charge reversal has to take a good part of one cycle to travel down the wire, which is what sets a useful length of the order of a quarter wavelength. A stub too short to hold a significant fraction of a cycle never builds a field at all, so it radiates almost nothing and the set receives almost nothing.

questions.explanation: Radiation requires oscillating fields, and oscillation requires enough electrical length for the reversal of the current to be felt along the whole conductor. This is the practical reason the same set works well on long-wave stations, where the quarter wavelength is metres rather than centimetres, and badly on short wavelengths with a short aerial. Matching the aerial length to the wavelength also keeps the feed line from reflecting the power back into the set.
questions.hint: Ask how long a current reversal takes to reach the far end of the wire.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why the charge stays on the outside of a hollow conductor
questions.learningObjective: explain why a charged hollow conductor keeps its charge on the outer surface
questions.stem: A hollow metal sphere is given a charge by touching it with a charged rod, and the rod is then taken well away. The sphere stays charged for as long as you care to wait. Explain in your own words why the charge cannot be found inside the metal and why it stays on the outside.

answer.exemplar: Any excess electron or missing electron inside the metal is free to move, so the moment such a charge appears in the bulk of the conductor it makes a field there, and that field immediately pushes the other free charges around. The redistribution continues until nothing inside is being pushed, and the only arrangement that achieves that is one with no field at all within the metal. The excess charge is therefore pushed out onto the surface, and because the sphere is hollow and closed, on the outer surface, leaving the cavity walls neutral. The charge is stable there precisely because there are no free charges left inside to rearrange, so there is nothing that could respond to a disturbance.

questions.explanation: The equilibrium condition does the work here: no field inside the metal, and therefore no charge inside the metal. The exterior field is unconstrained, so charge is free to sit on the outer surface where it makes a field in the space around the sphere. This is the same argument that makes a live conductor safe to touch only at its surface, and it is why an electric field exists in the cavity if a charge is placed there but never inside the metal.
questions.hint: Start from the condition that nothing inside the metal can still be moving.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a magnetic field bends a path without changing the speed
questions.learningObjective: explain why a magnetic force turns a path but does no work
questions.stem: A charged particle is fired into a uniform magnetic field at right angles to the field and curves round in a circle, and its speed stays the same the whole way round. Explain in your own words why the force bends the path without ever changing the speed.

answer.exemplar: The force is built from the charge, the velocity and the field with a sine of the angle between them, so at ninety degrees it is as large as it can be, and that direction is always across the direction of travel rather than along it. A force that acts only across the motion can rotate the velocity vector without changing its length, which is why the path bends and the speedometer needle never moves. Looked at around the circle, the particle slows on one side by exactly as much as it speeds up on the other, so over a full turn nothing has changed. The electric field is the opposite case, since it acts along the motion and there it changes the speed while leaving the direction alone.

questions.explanation: Work is done only by a force with a component along the displacement, and the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity at every point of the orbit, so the magnetic field does no work and the kinetic energy is untouched. That is what makes the circular orbit possible at constant speed, and it is the reason a magnetic field can steer and focus a beam of particles without ever changing how energetic they are.
questions.hint: Compare the direction of the force with the direction of the motion at every point.
